title: Chapter 1 · exercise 1
prompt: In one sentence each, state what a tokeniser does and what the model does. No jargon allowed.
answer: The tokeniser converts text into integer ids using a fixed vocabulary. The model takes ids and returns a probability for every possible next token.

title: Chapter 1 · exercise 2
prompt: A model's vocabulary is 65 tokens. What loss would it achieve if it guessed completely at random? (Chapter 3 gives you the formula; try it before reading on.)
answer: log(65) = 4.17 nats. Any loss at or above that means no learning at all.

title: Chapter 1 · exercise 3
prompt: Why does a model that predicts the next token appear to be able to translate between languages? What would it have needed to see in its training data?
answer: Translations appear side by side in its training text, so the same meaning in two languages becomes a predictable pattern. Without parallel text it cannot translate.

title: Chapter 1 · exercise 4
prompt: Your model outputs "The capital of France is" followed by "Lyon". Is that a bug in the code, the data, or neither? Explain in two sentences.
answer: Neither code nor data is broken. The model has no mechanism for truth - it produced the most likely continuation. Lyon was probably text-shaped in its training data.

title: Chapter 2 · exercise 1
prompt: Write down the shapes for a batch of 2 sequences, 16 tokens, 128-dim embedding, vocabulary 100 - at every row of the table above.
answer: raw (2, 16); embedding (2, 16, 128); with positions (2, 16, 128); after blocks (2, 16, 128); logits (2, 16, 100); loss ().

title: Chapter 2 · exercise 2
prompt: A model has 10 M parameters and you train on 100 M tokens. How many FLOPs? If your machine does 5 x 10^10 FLOP/s, how many hours is that?
answer: 6 x 1e7 x 1e8 = 6e15 FLOPs. At 5e10 FLOP/s that is 1.2e5 seconds, about 33 hours.

title: Chapter 2 · exercise 3
prompt: Why does the loss not change shape when you increase the number of layers?
answer: The loss is a single average over all positions. Depth changes its value, not its shape.

title: Chapter 2 · exercise 4
prompt: Which stage would you remove if you wanted a model that only ever predicts the single most likely next token, and what would break?
answer: Remove the softmax-and-sample stage and take the argmax of the logits directly. Nothing breaks; you lose variety and the ability to explore.

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 5
prompt: Compute softmax of [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]. What does the result tell you about a model that has learned nothing?
answer: All three are 1/3. Loss = log(3) = 1.099. A model at initialisation is exactly this uncertain, which is why its loss must equal log(V).

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 6
prompt: A model gives the correct token probability 0.05, with vocabulary 65. What is the loss, and how does it compare to guessing?
answer: Loss = -log(0.05) = 3.00. Better than the 4.17 baseline, but only by about one nat.

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 7
prompt: In the gradient descent table, what happens at learning rate 1.0? Work out steps 1 and 2 by hand.
answer: w1 = 0 - 1.0 x (-6) = 6, loss 9.0 - worse than the start. w2 = 6 - 1.0 x 6 = 0. It oscillates between 0 and 6 forever. Too large a step overshoots the minimum.

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 8
prompt: Why is the loss for a 50,257-token vocabulary higher than for a 65-token one, even for equally good models? Is that a fair comparison?
answer: Because log(50,257) = 10.83 versus log(65) = 4.17. Not directly comparable: to compare models with different vocabularies, subtract log(V) or compare perplexity per character.

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 9
prompt: If loss = -log(p), what probability corresponds to a loss of 1.0? To 0.5?

title: Chapter 3 · exercise 10
prompt: Explain to a friend, in three sentences and without the word "neural", why the loss decreasing means the model is getting better.
answer: Open answer. A good version: the model is being made to give the right continuation more often, so its average surprise about the next token falls, and lower surprise is what we mean by better language modelling.

title: Lab 1 · exercise 1
prompt: Print the 20 least frequent characters in the corpus. What happens to a message that contains one of them?
answer: They occur rarely, so the model barely learns them and will often confuse them. If a character is missing from the vocabulary entirely, encode raises KeyError - which is why real tokenisers fall back to bytes.

title: Lab 1 · exercise 2
prompt: Change range(60) to range(500) in the BPE loop. How many merges before the whole 4,000-character corpus becomes single tokens? Why is that bad?
answer: Around 200-300 merges on 4,000 characters, most words become one token. That is bad: each token is then seen once, so the model cannot generalise, and the vocabulary is specific to that exact file.

title: Lab 1 · exercise 3
prompt: Add a merge for a pair that does not exist in English (for example, q followed by z). What does the loop do?
answer: max() simply picks the next most frequent pair; there is no error. It only fails with ValueError when the vocabulary becomes empty and there are no pairs left.

title: Lab 1 · exercise 4
prompt: Decode this id sequence and write your own one-liner to encode it back: [20, 43, 50, 50, 53, 39].
answer: It decodes to Hello plus one punctuation character. Re-encoding returns the same id list - which is the property to test on every tokeniser you write.

title: Lab 2 · exercise 1
prompt: Change the learning rate to 30.0. What happens to the loss, and why does it happen within fifty steps?
answer: The loss explodes to NaN within a few dozen steps. Each step overshoots the minimum by more than the distance to it, exactly as in Chapter 3's example at learning rate 1.0.

title: Lab 2 · exercise 2
prompt: Set the learning rate to 0.01. How many steps until the loss reaches 3.0? Predict before you run.
answer: At lr 0.01 the first 200 steps barely move the loss; it needs thousands of steps to reach 3.0. Slow but stable - the trade-off you spend the rest of your life tuning.

title: Lab 2 · exercise 3
prompt: Train on text[:2000] instead of 20,000 characters. Does the val loss go up or down? Explain what that tells you about corpus size.
answer: Validation loss goes up. You have ten times less data, so the model memorises the training slice and the held-out tail gets worse.

title: Lab 2 · exercise 4
prompt: Print the five most likely continuations of the character (space). Do they match your intuition about English?
answer: On the 20,000-character slice: t (404), a (255), h (203), w (194), s (185). That is word-initial statistics, not language.

title: Lab 2 · exercise 5
prompt: Remove the - logits.max(...) line and use a larger W initialisation (standard deviation 5.0). What breaks, and why?
answer: exp overflows to infinity, infinity divided by infinity is NaN, and every subsequent gradient is NaN. The max subtraction is what keeps exp arguments negative.

title: Lab 3 · exercise 1
prompt: Delete the mask line and train for 200 steps. The loss drops almost to zero. Sample from the model and explain what you get.
answer: The loss collapses towards zero because each position can see its own target. At inference the mask is still needed, but the model has learned nothing about prediction - it learned to copy. Output is degenerate.

title: Lab 3 · exercise 2
prompt: Set n_head=1 and n_head=8 with the same total width. Which has more parameters? Which trains faster per step, and why?
answer: Parameter count is identical (4d squared either way). Speed is close; more heads means smaller matrices per head, so the arithmetic is the same but overhead rises slightly.

title: Lab 3 · exercise 3
prompt: In the worked example, what would row 0 look like without the mask?
answer: Softmax over [0.39, -0.51, -0.15] = [0.464, 0.189, 0.348]. Token 0 would spread its attention, including into the future.

title: Lab 3 · exercise 4
prompt: Print the attention weights for a 6-token input at inference. Can you find a head that attends to the previous token?
answer: Empirical. Look for heads whose attention sits one position left of the diagonal.

title: Lab 4 · exercise 1
prompt: Set n_layer=1 and n_layer=8. How much does the parameter count change? What does that tell you about where the width versus the depth costs sit?
answer: Each block adds 12d squared + 13d, about 790k at d = 256. Going from 1 to 8 layers adds roughly 5.5 M parameters - so depth is as expensive as width.

title: Lab 4 · exercise 2
prompt: Break the shape invariant on purpose: change nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd) to nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd + 1). Read the error message and learn to recognise it - you will see it again.
answer: It complains about a shape mismatch in LayerNorm's input. Read the expected versus actual shape in the message; that skill transfers to every other error.

title: Lab 4 · exercise 3
prompt: Why would removing self.ln_f change the model's behaviour at depth 12 but barely at depth 2?
answer: Deep stacks accumulate magnitude through many residual additions, so the final normalisation matters more as depth grows. At depth 2 it barely matters.

title: Lab 4 · exercise 4
prompt: Comment out the + self.wpe(pos). Train for 100 steps and sample. What is missing from the output?
answer: Without position embeddings the model cannot tell where a token is, so it treats the sequence as a bag. Output loses all ordering and line structure.

title: Lab 6 · exercise 1
prompt: Set temperature to 0.01 and generate 300 tokens. Describe the output and explain it using the table above.
answer: Temperature 0.01 makes the distribution nearly one-hot, so it is greedy and loops. The model is not broken; the sampler is deterministic.

title: Lab 6 · exercise 2
prompt: Set top_k = 1. How does the output compare to greedy? They should be identical - explain why.
answer: Identical. Top-k with k = 1 keeps only the argmax, which is the definition of greedy.

title: Lab 6 · exercise 3
prompt: Generate the same prompt five times at T = 1.0. How many distinct outputs do you get? Now at T = 0.3. Why does the number change?
answer: At T = 1 you get several distinct outputs; at T = 0.3 usually one or two. Lower temperature narrows the distribution, so repeated sampling converges on the same text.

title: Lab 6 · exercise 4
prompt: Find a prompt that makes your model loop. Is the loop a property of the model or of the sampler? What would fix it at each level?
answer: The loop is a property of both. The model provides a repeating distribution; the sampler decides whether repetition is reinforced. Fix at the sampler level first (temperature, top-p), at the model level only if the corpus itself repeats.
